assessment:
In this study, Benkeder and colleagues address a fundamental challenge in microglial biology: how to objectively and comprehensively characterize the diverse morphologies that microglia exhibit across different physiological and pathological states. The authors argue convincingly that current approaches—which rely on categorical classification of microglia into discrete morphotypes (ramified, amoeboid, reactive, etc.)—are biologically inappropriate because microglial morphology exists along a continuum rather than in distinct groups. To address this limitation, they developed MorphoCellSorter, an open-source computational tool that ranks individual microglia along a morphological continuum using principal component analysis (PCA) to identify the most discriminant parameters from 20 computed morphological indices, followed by Andrews plots to generate an objective ranking.

The methodological approach is rigorous and well-validated. The authors first demonstrate the limitations of k-means clustering on a rat stroke model, showing that the resulting clusters are morphologically heterogeneous and that approximately 60% of cells don't fit cleanly into predefined categories. They then develop their ranking approach and validate it against manual expert rankings, achieving high Spearman correlations (0.96-0.97) that match or exceed inter-expert agreement (0.93). Importantly, they test the tool's generalizability across five diverse datasets encompassing different species (rat, mouse), ages (embryonic to adult), experimental conditions (in vivo, in vitro, ex vivo), imaging modalities (confocal, two-photon, widefield, brightfield), and pathological contexts (stroke, Alzheimer's disease, congenital central hypoventilation syndrome). The tool successfully detects morphological alterations in the Alzheimer's model (16.4% overlap between disease and control) while appropriately identifying no differences in the embryonic CCHS model (78.9% overlap), demonstrating both sensitivity and specificity.

The strength of this work lies in its conceptual innovation—replacing arbitrary categorization with continuous ranking—and its practical implementation as an accessible, automated tool that works across diverse experimental contexts. The authors are appropriately transparent about limitations, including the use of 2D projections rather than full 3D reconstructions and the dependence on segmentation quality. While the tool doesn't provide the precise 3D measurements available from other specialized software, it fills an important niche as a rapid, objective screening method. The open-source availability and demonstrated broad applicability position MorphoCellSorter as a potentially valuable standardization tool for the field. However, the lack of systematic evaluation of how imaging resolution or segmentation quality affects ranking accuracy represents a gap in the validation, and the biological interpretation of why certain parameters are consistently selected while others are never selected could be explored more deeply.
